newsitem.title: UK: UK stock market hopes for year-end rally fade.
newsitem.headline: UK stock market hopes for year-end rally fade.

text.p: The London stock market is headed towards the end of the year beset by Wall Street weakness and with increasing doubts as to whether investors can count on a traditional year-end market rally.
Just one week since the global melt-down of "frantic Friday", British shares were again under threat on Friday 13th, thanks to another 100-point fall on the Dow.
At its worst the FTSE was down 56 points on Friday. "If there is going to be a bad day Friday 13th is the day to have it," said Nick Glydon a chartist at Robert Fleming Securities.
During the white-knuckle ride of the past few sessions the U.S. stock average has dropped 3.3 percent in two weeks, raising fears that a major correction is looming.
"The American market is the most overvalued in world-wide terms," Vanessa James, director UK equities at Legal and General told Reuters Financial TV on Friday.
Meanwhile the FTSE has lost 2.7 percent in the last week, continuing to be dragged back from record highs of 4,053 reached at the end of October, just before an interest rate rise.

But some analysts still expect the market to finish the year on a more bullish note, noting that whereas New York has seen a massive 33 percent rise in blue-chips this year, London is still lagging behind with gains of 9.9 percent.
"The first two weeks of December trading are not usually great," said Glydon. "It's really mid-December when things start to pick up. So far there's nothing particularly wrong with this December."

Glydon commented that since 1969 London's all-share index has risen in 70 percent of all December's and 78 percent of January's. But he admitted that "the risk is on the downside for the next couple of trading days." Sharon Quinn, a chart watcher at MMS International said the recent volatility had not disturbed the underlying bullish trend, but added that 3,900 is the level that must be held for the trend to remain unbroken.

"We failed to break 4,100, and potentially we now have a double top formation unfolding, with support at 3,900 the critical level to watch," Quinn said. "A close below this level would indicate further weakness to test support at 3,800."

There are few scheduled economic or corporate features next week to help boost sentiment and switch attention back to the domestic market, so all eyes are likely to remain focused on the other side of the Atlantic.

Among major company news next week, half-year earnings from East Midlands Electricity and MFI Furniture Group Plc are due on Monday. Thursday will see the Asda supermarket group report its interim results.
Economic statistics will include November retail sales and unemployment figures which are expected only to confirm recent robust trends in the economy.
Ciaran Barr of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell expects "a week of real economy data that will shed little fresh light on the growth outlook."

Yet in the U.S. a batch of data showing trends for December will keep nerves jangling. The Philadelphia Fed index, a measure of consumer sentiment will provide the most recent glimpse of what December has in store for the world's biggest economy.
